target_customer: Employers of any size (initially tech companies) that buy fertility and family-building benefits for staff
problem: Fertility care is expensive and confusing, and most employers offered no fertility benefit. Employees paid tens of thousands of dollars out of pocket for egg freezing or IVF.
business_model: B2B employer-paid benefit platform, per-employer fees plus reimbursement administration

founders.name: Tammy Sun
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch (Sept 2017) says she froze her eggs while working at Evernote, which had no fertility benefit, and that this inspired Carrot. Education not found in sources opened.

founders.name: Asima Ahmad
founders.background_notes: Listed as founder and CMO on the YC page and as co-founder on the Carrot Series C post. Background not found in sources opened.

competitors.name: Progyny
competitors.what: Fertility benefits manager selling IVF and egg-freezing coverage to large self-insured employers
competitors.traction_then: Launched to market in 2016 with 5 employers covering 110,000 lives per its own timeline
competitors.funding_then: $10M Series B extension in May 2017; CNBC cited more than $85M raised

technical_complexity.rationale: A benefits administration and provider-network product with payments and reimbursement. Standard software engineering; the hard parts were operational (clinic networks, claims handling) rather than technical.

defensibility.rationale: Employer contracts and provider networks create some lock-in once benefits are in place, but the core idea was copyable and several rivals existed.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Progyny went public in 2019 and remained a rival. As of the Nasdaq Private Market page Carrot is still private with no acquisition.

market_need_then: In 2017 only a few large tech employers such as Apple and Facebook covered egg freezing, per TechCrunch. Founder Tammy Sun paid about $30,000 out of pocket while at Evernote, which had no such benefit, and employers were using fertility coverage as a recruiting tool.

branding.domain_note: Company site is get-carrot.com, a prefixed domain rather than carrot.com.

identity.voice_and_tone: Warm and inclusive, per the company site language on culturally competent care

brand_strength.rationale: Little brand-specific press was found. The name is simple and friendly, but nothing sourced shows the brand itself driving growth.

outcome_analysis: Carrot rode a shift in employer attitudes toward fertility benefits, with a founder who had personally paid for egg freezing and a clean sequence of rounds from a 2017 seed through a 2021 Series C led by Tiger Global. It remains independent and private. Third party sources report a small layoff event in early 2024 and no new priced round since 2021, so growth since the Series C is unclear.
notes: Series A of $11.5M led by CRV is from a Trusted Insight item and search summaries, not opened directly. Series B article states $40M total raised, which exceeds the sum of seed and Series A, consistent with the recorded rounds. Series C post is dated July 2022 on the page but Forbes coverage is Aug 2021. Aggregator valuation figures ($345M, $611M) conflict and are not recorded. A 2024 layoff is reported only by TrueUp and BuiltIn snippets. Carrot's relationship to Maven: Maven Ventures was an investor.
